meta.descriptionEn: On the morning of 21 October 1966, children in a Welsh mining village had only just begun their lessons when a mountain of colliery waste above them gave way. In minutes, a river of black slurry reached Pantglas Junior School. Why was a giant coal tip built over a spring? Why were residents' complaints about flooding and sludge ignored? And who was really to blame? This documentary follows the rescue by miners and villagers, the long public tribunal, the bitter fight over a charity fund, and the safety laws that followed. A story of engineering neglect, official failure and a community's grief, told using the official record.

articleEn: It was the morning of 21 October 1966 in the Welsh village of Aberfan. The children had arrived at school, and the last day of lessons before the half-term break was getting under way. Then, at 9:15 am, a black wave came down the hillside. It was Tip 7, a huge heap of coal waste, and it suddenly began to flow.

The water-laden mud and debris moved at 11 to 21 miles per hour, in waves 20 to 30 feet high. The flow struck Pantglas Junior School. In the disaster, 116 children and 28 adults lost their lives. We remember them all with respect.

Several questions drive this story. Why was such a huge heap of coal waste built directly above a village? Was there any earlier sign of the danger? Were warnings made but not heard? And finally, who was held responsible? These three questions are the foundation of this account.

In what follows, we look at how the village grew, where Tip 7 was placed, and what the inquiry later concluded. This is not only the story of one accident. It is a story of ignorance, wrong decisions and failures to pass on information. Let us begin at the start.

articleEn: Aberfan is a small village in Wales, about 4 miles south of Merthyr Tydfil. It sits on the slopes of the Taff Valley, in the shadow of Mynydd Merthyr. Its story starts in 1869. On 23 August, John Nixon and his partners began digging Merthyr Vale Colliery. At that time Aberfan had only two small cottages and an inn, where local farmers and bargemen came to sit. The colliery changed everything. By 1966 the population was about 5,000, and most people worked in the coal industry.

The River Taff runs through the area from north to south. On the western side, an old canal bed and a disused railway embankment run parallel to it. In 1947 Britain's coal industry was nationalised. On 1 January, notices went up at every colliery saying it was now managed by the National Coal Board. The notice read: 'This colliery is now managed by the National Coal Board on behalf of the people.'

The NCB took over 958 collieries at once. At the start it had about 800,000 workers, around 4 percent of Britain's whole workforce. The mines it inherited varied in size, and in 1947 more than a third of them produced less than 100,000 tons of coal a year.

Oversight of the mines belonged to HM Inspectorate of Mines. Interestingly, these inspectors had been engineers in the coal industry, and they were also former NCB employees. So the body they were supposed to supervise was one they had old ties with.

Now consider the NCB's own situation. In the late 1950s, competition from cheap oil began, and from 1957 the coal industry started to shrink. Between 1958 and 1959, 85 collieries closed. In 1960 Alf Robens became NCB chairman. His policy was to focus on the most productive pits. Over ten years productivity rose by 70 percent, but pits and workforce grew fewer.

So by 1966, Aberfan's livelihood, its mines and their waste were all in the hands of one organisation, the NCB. The waste from the mines kept piling up on the mountain. How many heaps were there, where were they, and how were they built? That is the subject of the next chapter.

articleEn: The waste from the mines, known as spoil, was dumped on the mountain. In the 1910s the first tip was started on the western slope, above the river and the village. By 1966 there were seven tips holding about 2.6 million cubic yards of waste. All of them stood directly above the village. Tips 4 and 5 sat like mounds on the crest of the slope, and the other five were below them.

Only Tip 7 was still in use. It was begun in 1958, and at the time of the disaster it stood 111 feet high. It held 297,000 cubic yards of spoil, including 30,000 cubic yards of tailings. Tailings are fine particles of coal and ash. When wet, they behave like quicksand. Remember this, because it later became a point of debate.

The most important matter was water. Tips 4, 5 and 7 were built over streams or springs. Tip 7 was partly on ground where springs emerged, which went against the NCB's own procedures. The springs were no secret. They were common knowledge in the area, and had been marked on Ordnance Survey and Geological Society maps since 1874.

An earlier warning had also come long before. Tip 4 was used from 1933 to 1945 and was started on boggy ground between two streams. When it was planned, the Merthyr Tydfil borough engineer thought that, despite the site, the tip was unlikely to form an avalanche. Then, in the early 1940s, there was ground movement, and in 1944 a drainage channel was dug. Even so, in November that year part of the tip slipped. It travelled 1,600 feet downhill and stopped about 500 feet above the village. So the closeness of the danger had already been shown.

The tribunal later found that no survey of the tips had ever been made. They had been added to continually, in a disordered way and without planning. According to the tribunal, the basic cause was a complete absence of a tipping policy. The NCB was following in the footsteps of its predecessors. Neither the Inspectorate nor the law gave any guidance. The tribunal noted that only part of West Germany and South Africa had laws on tip safety. Responsibility for the tips lay with mechanical engineers, who had only a layman's understanding of tip stability.
Did warning bells ring? The next chapter looks at that.

articleEn: In May 1963, Tip 7 slipped slightly. In November of that year there was a much larger slide. Did anyone take notice? The NCB said it was not a slide. In its account, it was a tailings run, meaning a flow of tailings from the surface of the tip that did not affect its stability. After this the NCB stopped putting tailings on Tip 7, but ordinary spoil was still tipped there.

Now look at the weather. Aberfan averages 60 inches of rain a year. In 1960 it was 70.5 inches, the highest in the years before the disaster. Between 1952 and 1965, Pantglas flooded at least 11 times. Residents said the water was black and left a slippery layer when it went down. They complained to Merthyr Tydfil County Borough Council. From July 1963 to March 1964, letters passed between the Council and the NCB. The subject was 'Danger from Coal Slurry being tipped at the rear of the Pantglas Schools.'

In early 1965 the Council and the NCB held meetings. The Board promised that blocked pipes and drainage ditches, which were behind the flooding, would be repaired. But by October 1966, when the tip fell, no action had been taken. The promise stayed on paper.

None of this was hidden. Everyone locally knew about the springs, and they had been on maps since 1874. Aberfan's MP, S. O. Davies, later told the tribunal that for years he had feared the tip might slip and reach the village. But he did not speak up. His reason was that he was quite sure the colliery would be closed. The tribunal did not accept his evidence. It doubted that he had fully understood the weight of his words.

The tribunal said that with proper inquiry, the course of events might have changed dramatically and decisively. But the warnings were ignored. They were there: slides, floods, complaints, meetings. The question was whether anyone was listening. And then came the morning of 21 October 1966.

articleEn: In the first three weeks of October, 6.5 inches of rain fell, about half of it in the third week alone. Then, in the night of 20 to 21 October, the crest of Tip 7 sank 9 to 10 feet. The rails used to carry spoil also fell into the hollow. At 7:30 am the morning shift workers saw this. One worker went to the colliery and returned with the tips supervisor. It was decided that no more work would be done that day, and that a new tipping site would be chosen the following week. Our sources make no mention of any warning given to the village.

The children had reached school on the last day before half-term. At 9:15 am the water-laden debris broke away from Tip 7 and began to flow downhill. Its speed on the way down was 11 to 21 miles per hour, in waves 20 to 30 feet high. Consultant engineer G. M. J. Williams told the tribunal that the movement took the wet material beyond the point of liquefaction. Then, almost at once, the lower wet part of the tip turned from a solid into a heavy fluid, about twice as dense as water.

About 140,000 cubic yards of spoil came down 700 yards. On the way it destroyed two farm cottages, and the people living there were killed. About 50,000 cubic yards crossed the canal and railway embankment and entered the village. Two water mains broke, and the extra water soaked the debris further. Those who heard it said it sounded like a low-flying jet or thunder.

The debris hit Pantglas Junior School on Moy Road. The children had arrived only a few minutes before, and the teachers had just begun taking the register. Of 240 children present at the school, 109 died, along with 5 teachers. In the nearby streets 18 houses were destroyed. When the debris stopped, it set solid again. A heap of slurry up to 30 feet high stood blocking the road. The neighbouring secondary school was also affected.

Some staff tried to save the children. School meals clerk Nansi Williams shielded five children with her own body, and all five survived. But Nansi Williams herself did not. She had a pound note on her, which she had been collecting as lunch money. Deputy headmaster Dai Beynon tried to protect himself and five children with a blackboard. He and all 34 children in his class died.

When the debris stopped, the noise stopped too. One resident remembered that in that silence there was no bird to be heard, and no voice of a child. Right after the silence, the people of the village ran towards the school. What happened next is told in the next chapter.

articleEn: As soon as the debris stopped, villagers ran to the school. They began to remove the debris with their hands and garden tools. At 9:25 am Merthyr Tydfil police received a phone call. A local person reported that there had been a landslide at Pantglas and that the tip had come down on the school. Within 20 minutes the first miners from Aberfan colliery arrived, called up from the coal seams. They guided the first digging. The miners knew that disorganised digging could make the debris settle, so they worked in organised groups under the supervision of pit managers.

At 9:50 am the first injured reached St Tydfil's Hospital. More people were brought in before 11:00 am, but after that no one was found alive. The news was the first item in the 10:30 am BBC news summary. As a result, thousands of volunteers arrived in Aberfan to help. Their intentions were good, but their efforts often got in the way of experienced miners and trained rescue teams.

Meanwhile, water from the two broken mains kept flowing into the debris. Only at 11:30 am did the water authorities manage to shut off the supply. It is estimated that the mains added 2 to 3 million imperial gallons of water to the debris. At 12:00 pm NCB engineers began digging a drainage channel. Within two hours the water was diverted to a safe place, so that an attempt could be made to stabilise the tip.

The village's Bethania Chapel was made into a temporary mortuary. Because space was tight, parents were called in one at a time to identify their children. 400 embalmers offered to help as volunteers. A group from Northern Ireland removed the seats from their plane so that small coffins could be brought in.

Secretary of State for Wales Cledwyn Hughes arrived at 4:00 pm and phoned Prime Minister Harold Wilson. Wilson said Hughes should do whatever was necessary, even if normal procedures or costs and legal limits stood in the way. Wilson himself arrived at 9:40 that night.

Lord Robens, the NCB chairman, did not go to the scene that day. In the evening he attended a ceremony for becoming chancellor of the University of Surrey. When Hughes made contact, NCB officials wrongly said that Robens was himself overseeing the relief work. Robens arrived on the evening of the following day. In a television interview the next morning, he said it was impossible for his people to have known of a spring inside the tip. But the springs had been on maps since 1874. Desmond Ackner, counsel for the families, later called the statement a public scandal.

The next morning Lord Snowdon visited, and at 11:00 am Prince Philip toured the site and spoke to the workers. On 27 October, 81 children and one woman were buried together in Bryntaf Cemetery. 10,000 people attended. Because of the amount and hardness of the debris, the search took a week to complete. The last victim was found on 28 October. On 29 October the Queen and the Duke of Edinburgh came to Aberfan to pay their respects. In all, 144 people died, 116 of them children.
Now the question was simple: who was responsible? A high-level inquiry had by then been set up.

articleEn: After resolutions in both Houses of Parliament, the Secretary of State for Wales appointed a tribunal. The sources differ on the date: one gives 25 October and another 26 October, so we mention both. The chairman was Lord Justice Edmund Davies, a respected Welsh judge who was born about two miles from Aberfan and went to school in Mountain Ash. With him were civil engineer Harold Harding and Vernon Lawrence, a former Clerk of Monmouthshire County Council. Professor Alan Bishop handled the geotechnical research. Before the proceedings began, the Attorney General warned the media that those commenting on these matters could face consequences such as contempt of court.

The tribunal sat for 76 days, at the time the longest inquiry of its kind in British history. 136 witnesses gave evidence, 300 exhibits were examined and 2.5 million words of testimony were heard. This included mining history and geological conditions. According to the report, the tribunal would have saved a great deal of time if the NCB had not resisted every hint of responsibility. On the 49th day an NCB witness admitted for the first time that the tip safety arrangements were inadequate. On the 65th day another witness admitted that the instability of Tip 7 could have been foreseen. This contradicted Lord Robens's claims.

Then Robens was called. He said that before the inquiry began he knew that the tip's instability could have been foreseen. In cross-examination his answers were contradictory. The NCB's counsel asked the tribunal to disregard Robens's evidence, and that is what happened.

The tribunal ended its hearings on 28 April 1967 and published its report on 3 August 1967. Its basic conclusion was that the disaster could and should have been prevented. It was not a story of wickedness but of ignorance and incompetence. Those choosing tip sites were ignorant, those supervising were unqualified, and those with knowledge did not pass it on.

According to the report, the blame lay with the NCB. It was spread in different degrees among NCB headquarters, the South Western Divisional Board and certain individuals. The basic cause was the complete absence of a tipping policy. At that time, apart from part of West Germany and South Africa, nowhere had any law on tip safety.

Questions were also raised about tailings. The tribunal said that according to expert evidence a large slide would have happened even without tailings, so they were not the cause. Nine NCB employees were assigned varying degrees of responsibility. No blame fell on Merthyr Tydfil Council or the NUM. According to the report, this was because they believed the NCB was following correct technical advice. The report gave an analogy: many witnesses were unaware of what was before their eyes, like asking moles about the habits of birds. According to McLean and Johnes, HM Inspectorate of Mines was hardly challenged at the tribunal, even though it was an example of regulatory capture.

articleEn: Now for the most bitter part. No case was brought against the NCB and no fine was imposed. No NCB staff member was demoted, dismissed or prosecuted. One witness who had been criticised by the inquiry had been promoted to a board-level post. Margaret Thatcher raised this in parliament. After the report, Robens spoke to the Minister of Power, Richard Marsh, and offered his resignation. But Marsh and Prime Minister Harold Wilson did not accept it. According to Ronald Dearing, Robens was steering the coal industry through difficult contraction without major strikes, and he also had the support of industry and union. Papers released in 1997 showed that Robens first agreed to the wording of a letter and then offered his resignation. Leo Abse called it a graceless pavane.

At first the NCB offered the affected families £50. Later this became £500, which the NCB called a good offer. Many families found it inadequate. On the other side, public sympathy poured in. About 88,000 donations arrived, and the fund reached £1.75 million. But in 1967 the Charity Commission said that giving money to parents might be against the trust deed. Later, £5,000 per family was allowed on conditions. For children who were not physically injured but were under mental strain, the commission called payments quite illegal. This decision affected 340 children.

The remaining tips still posed a danger above the village. Residents petitioned George Thomas and put a small heap of coal slurry on the table of the Welsh Office. Robens told the Treasury that the cost would be about £3 million and that the NCB would not pay. The Treasury also refused to pay. In the end £150,000 was taken from the fund for the removal. The NCB paid £350,000, and the government paid the rest. The final cost was £850,000. The trustees agreed to the demand because there was no other way to get the tips removed. S. O. Davies alone opposed it and resigned in protest. Political scientists Jacint Jordana and David Levi-Faur regard the payment as unquestionably unlawful under charity law. At the time the Charity Commission had not objected.

The disaster also affected people's health. According to a 2003 study, half of the survivors had PTSD at some point in life. One doctor wrote that by every statistic this was a village of excessive sickness. But within five years the birth rate also rose. In 1997 the British government returned £150,000. But this did not include inflation or interest, which would then have come to about £1.5 million. Then in February 2007 the Welsh Government gave £1.5 million to the Aberfan Memorial Charity and £500,000 to the Aberfan Education Charity. Thus a total of £2 million was repaid.
The question was whether, despite no punishment, anything changed after the disaster. The next section looks at that.

articleEn: In 1969 the government passed the Mines and Quarries (Tips) Act. Its aim was to fill the gap in the rules for mine and quarry spoil tips. The act extended the Mines and Quarries Act 1954, which had not applied to tips. The tribunal's recommendation was meant to fill this very gap. But McLean and Johnes say that the broad public safety commitment the tribunal wanted was not fully put into effect by the act.

In May 1970 Barbara Castle made Robens chairman of the Committee on Health and Safety at Work. This was the same Robens who had been NCB chairman at the time of Aberfan. In 1972 the committee's Robens Report was published. As a result came the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974, and the Health and Safety Executive was set up.

In March 1973 the Queen opened the Aberfan Memorial Garden. It stands on the site of Pantglas Junior School, and its stone walls show where the classrooms were. Merthyr Vale Colliery closed in 1989. In 1997 the Queen and the Duke of Edinburgh planted a tree in the Memorial Garden. In October 2016, events were held in the garden and cemetery for the 50th anniversary. The Prince of Wales represented the Queen, and ministers were present too. In February 2022 the cemetery, memorial garden and the slide path of the tip were entered in the Register of Parks and Gardens of Special Historic Interest in Wales. The record describes the place as having great national importance and meaning. In January 2022 an appeal was also made for a permanent home for salvaged artefacts.

Huw Edwards wrote that the lessons of Aberfan remain important today: public accountability, responsibility, competence and transparency. One lesson of this story is that when people complain again and again, they should be listened to seriously. Aberfan's residents had complained about flooding. A second lesson is that whoever has knowledge should pass it on. The tribunal mentioned the failure of communication. The third lesson is about oversight. According to McLean and Johnes, the regulator operated in the interest of the very body it was supposed to oversee, rather than the public.

Some questions remain open today. When an organisation faces its own mistake, how is accountability completed? And can compensation and repayment ever be enough? If you liked this documentary, please like and subscribe, and tell us in the comments what the biggest lesson from Aberfan is for you.

shorts.titleEn: The Black Wave That Hit a School at 9:15 am
shorts.text: صبح 9:15 بجے پہاڑ سے ایک کالی لہر نیچے آئی۔ کیا آپ سوچ سکتے ہیں کہ ایک کوئلے کا ڈھیر پورے گاؤں کے لیے خطرہ بن گیا؟ تاریخ تھی 21 October 1966۔ Wales کے گاؤں Aberfan میں بچے half-term سے پہلے آخری دن school پہنچ چکے تھے۔ پھر Tip 7 سے پانی سے بھرا ہوا ملبہ ٹوٹا اور نیچے بہنے لگا۔ یہ 11 سے 21 miles per hour کی رفتار سے آیا، اور لہریں 20 سے 30 feet اونچی تھیں۔ یہ سیلاب Pantglas Junior School سے ٹکرایا۔ اس حادثے میں 116 بچے اور 28 بالغ افراد جان سے گئے۔ ہم ان سب کو احترام سے یاد کرتے ہیں۔ لیکن سوال یہ ہے کہ کوئلے کا اتنا بڑا ڈھیر گاؤں کے عین اوپر کیوں بنایا گیا تھا؟ کیا خطرے کی پہلے سے کوئی نشانی موجود تھی؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Subah 9:15 baje pahaar se ek kali lehar neeche aayi. Kya aap soch sakte hain ke ek koyle ka dhair poore gaon ke liye khatra ban gaya? Tareekh thi 21 October 1966. Wales ke gaon Aberfan mein bachay half-term se pehle aakhri din school pahunch chukay thay. Phir Tip 7 se pani se bhara hua malba toota aur neeche behne laga. Yeh 11 se 21 miles per hour ki raftar se aaya, aur lehrain 20 se 30 feet unchi thin. Yeh sailab Pantglas Junior School se takraya. Is haadsay mein 116 bachay aur 28 baligh afraad jaan se gaye. Hum in sab ko ehteram se yaad karte hain. Lekin sawal yeh hai ke koyle ka itna bara dhair gaon ke ain oopar kyun banaya gaya tha? Kya khatray ki pehle se koi nishani maujood thi? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

shorts.titleEn: Aberfan: The Warnings Nobody Heeded Before 1966
shorts.text: کیا Aberfan کی tragedy سے پہلے warning مل چکی تھی؟ May 1963 میں Tip 7 تھوڑا سا کھسک گیا۔ اسی سال November میں اس سے کہیں بڑی slide ہوئی۔ NCB نے کہا کہ یہ slide نہیں تھی۔ ان کے مطابق یہ tailings run تھا، یعنی tip کی سطح سے tailings کا بہاؤ، جس سے استحکام متاثر نہیں ہوا۔ اس کے بعد tailings ڈالنا بند ہوا، مگر عام spoil پھر بھی ڈالا جاتا رہا۔ اب موسم دیکھیں۔ Aberfan میں سالانہ اوسطاً 60 inches بارش ہوتی ہے۔ 1952 سے 1965 کے درمیان Pantglas میں کم از کم 11 بار سیلاب آیا۔ رہائشیوں نے شکایت کی کہ پانی کالا تھا۔ انہوں نے Merthyr Tydfil کی council سے رابطہ کیا۔ تو کیا کسی نے ان کی بات سنی؟ جواب آپ کو چونکا دے گا۔ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Kya Aberfan ki tragedy se pehle warning mil chuki thi? May 1963 mein Tip 7 thora sa khisak gaya. Isi saal November mein is se kahin bari slide hui. NCB ne kaha ke yeh slide nahin thi. Un ke mutabiq yeh tailings run tha, yaani tip ki satah se tailings ka bahao, jis se istehkam mutasir nahin hua. Is ke baad tailings dalna band hua, magar aam spoil phir bhi dala jata raha. Ab mausam dekhein. Aberfan mein salana ausatan 60 inches barish hoti hai. 1952 se 1965 ke darmiyan Pantglas mein kam az kam 11 baar sailab aaya. Rehaishiyon ne shikayat ki ke pani kala tha. Unhon ne Merthyr Tydfil ki council se rabta kiya. To kya kisi ne un ki baat suni? Jawab aap ko chaunka dega. Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:

Did anyone act on the warnings?

shorts.titleEn: Aberfan: No Punishment and the Fund Taken
shorts.text: Aberfan کی کہانی کا سب سے کڑوا حصہ یہ ہے کہ کسی کو سزا نہیں ملی۔ NCB پر نہ مقدمہ چلا، نہ جرمانہ ہوا۔ کسی NCB staff کو demote، برطرف یا prosecute بھی نہیں کیا گیا۔ ایک witness، جس پر inquiry نے تنقید کی تھی، board level کے عہدے پر ترقی پا چکا تھا۔ Margaret Thatcher نے parliament میں یہ بات اٹھائی۔ report کے بعد Lord Robens نے Minister of Power Richard Marsh سے بات کی اور استعفے کی پیشکش کی۔ مگر Marsh اور Prime Minister Harold Wilson نے اسے قبول نہیں کیا۔ پھر ایک اور بات سامنے آئی۔ باقی tips ہٹانے کے لیے disaster fund سے £150,000 لیے گئے۔ 1997 میں یہ رقم واپس کی گئی۔ تو آخر Robens کا استعفا کیسے طے ہوا تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Aberfan ki kahani ka sab se karwa hissa yeh hai ke kisi ko saza nahin mili. NCB par na muqadma chala, na jurmana hua. Kisi NCB staff ko demote, bartaraf ya prosecute bhi nahin kiya gaya. Ek witness, jis par inquiry ne tanqeed ki thi, board level ke ohde par taraqqi pa chuka tha. Margaret Thatcher ne parliament mein yeh baat uthayi. Report ke baad Lord Robens ne Minister of Power Richard Marsh se baat ki aur istifay ki peshkash ki. Magar Marsh aur Prime Minister Harold Wilson ne ise qabool nahin kiya. Phir ek aur baat samne aayi. Baqi tips hatane ke liye disaster fund se £150,000 liye gaye. 1997 mein yeh raqam wapas ki gayi. To aakhir Robens ka istifa kaise tay hua tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
No one was prosecuted, and £150,000 was taken from the disaster fund for tip removal.
It was repaid in 1997.
